whisper.label: Whisper Large-V3
whisper.text:
My name is Julian Day and this is my good friend and colleague Mari Carter.
This is our first collaboration together, our first formal collaboration.
It's called Blissville and it's a work in two parts.
A large light work that you see behind us and also an associated video work.
The work behind us that you see is a conglomerate of nine letters and the letters spell out
the phrase Homes Not Hotels which was some of the chants and signage in a 2018 protest
speaking about the fact that there were more homeless residents in the city of Blissville,
Queens than there were residents that lived there.
The overall work is a study I guess or a reflection on one of the really pressing issues that
New York City faces now but has been facing for decades and that is the way that property
and community and what we call gentrification impacts on a wide range of spaces.
Blissville was a town that was engineered to some extent in the 19th century as a kind
of utopian space.
It was a place for workers.
Over the decades it's become a lot more industrial and rugged and currently remains as a tiny
triangle of a mixture of houses and industrial spaces ringed by a giant motorway, a waterway
and a cemetery.
And so as a solution to homelessness it becomes this real hotspot, sort of a flash point in
the conversation.
I think that the space that we're in now in Long Island City is only about a 25 to 30
minute walk from Blissville itself.
We felt as though it was pretty important to not only be self-referential in the work
but to not be self-congratulatory in the work and speak directly about the issue at
hand which is gentrification in New York City and we wanted the work to kind of speak to
the homage of that situation as a whole.
I think that's what we're trying to do.
